entries.a0056f289131b82d9b9a4942cd9f4b0d0db9ec9c: <div sID="gen31723" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Gal.4" sID="Gal.4"/> <div eID="gen31723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31724" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31725" type="x-p"/> The apostle, in this chapter, is still carrying on the same general design as in the former—to recover these Christians from the impressions made upon them by the judaizing teachers, and to represent their weakness and folly in suffering themselves to be drawn away from the gospel doctrine of justification, and to be deprived of their freedom from the bondage of the law of Moses. For this purpose he makes use of various considerations; such as, I. The great excellence of the gospel state above the legal, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.1-Gal.4.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. The happy change that was made in them at their conversion, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.8-Gal.4.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. III. The affection they had had for him and his ministry, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.12-Gal.4.16">ver. 12-16</reference>. IV. The character of the false teachers by whom they had been perverted, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.17-Gal.4.18">ver. 17, 18</reference>. V. The very tender affection he had for them, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.19-Gal.4.20">ver. 19, 20</reference>. VI. The history of Isaac and Ishmael, by a comparison taken from which he illustrates the difference between such as rested in Christ and such as trusted in the law. And in all these, as he uses great plainness and faithfulness with them, so he expresses the tenderest concern for them.
entries.5e6b74537c7fa4f73d505b8187426c231deddda8: <div eID="gen31725" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31724" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Redemption by Christ. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31726" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now I say, <hi type="italic">That</hi> the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all; <hi type="super">2</hi> But is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father. <hi type="super">3</hi> Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world: <hi type="super">4</hi> But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, <hi type="super">5</hi> To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons. 6 And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father. <hi type="super">7</hi> Wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then a heir of God through Christ. <div eID="gen31726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31727" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle deals plainly with those who hearkened to the judaizing teachers, who cried up the law of Moses in competition with the gospel of Christ, and endeavored to bring them under the bondage of it. To convince them of their folly, and to rectify their mistake herein, in these verses he prosecutes the comparison of a child under age, which he had touched upon in the foregoing chapter, and thence shows what great advantages we have now, under the gospel, above what they had under the law. And here. <div eID="gen31727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31728" type="x-p"/> I. He acquaints us with the state of the Old-Testament church: it was like a child under age, and it was used accordingly, being kept in a state of darkness and bondage, in comparison of the greater light and liberty which we enjoy under the gospel. That was indeed a dispensation of grace, and yet it was comparatively a dispensation of darkness; for as the heir, in his minority, is <hi type="italic">under tutors and governors till the time appointed of his father,</hi> by whom he is educated and instructed in those things which at present he knows little of the meaning of, though afterwards they are likely to be of great use to him; so it was with the Old-Testament church—the Mosaic economy, which they were under, was what they could not fully understand the meaning of; for, as the apostle says (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">2 Cor. iii. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">They could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished.</hi> But to the church, when grown up to maturity, in gospel days, it becomes of great use. And as that was a dispensation of darkness, so of bondage too; for <hi type="italic">they were in bondage under the elements of the world,</hi> being tied to a great number of burdensome rites and observances, by which, as by a kind of first rudiments, they were taught and instructed, and whereby they were kept in a state of subjection, like a child under tutors and governors. The church then lay more under the character of <hi type="italic">a servant,</hi> being obliged to do every thing according to the command of God, without being fully acquainted with the reason of it; but the service under the gospel appears to be more reasonable than that was. The time appointed of the Father having come, when the church was to arrive at its full age, the darkness and bondage under which it before lay are removed, and we are under a dispensation of greater light and liberty. <div eID="gen31728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31729" type="x-p"/> II. He acquaints us with the much happier state of Christians under the gospel-dispensation, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.4-Gal.4.7">v. 4-7</reference>. <hi type="italic">When the fulness of time had come,</hi> the time appointed of the Father, when he would put an end to the legal dispensation, and set up another and a better in the room of it, <hi type="italic">he sent forth his Son,</hi> &c. The person who was employed to introduce this new dispensation was no other than the Son of God himself, the only-begotten of the Father, who, as he had been prophesied of and promised from the foundation of the world, so in due time he was manifested for this purpose. He, in pursuance of the great design he had undertaken, submitted to be <hi type="italic">made of a woman</hi>—there is his incarnation; and to be <hi type="italic">made under the law</hi>—there is his subjection. He who was truly God for our sakes became man; and he who was Lord of all consented to come into a state of subjection and to take upon him the form of a servant; and one great end of all this was <hi type="italic">to redeem those that were under the law</hi>—to save us from that intolerable yoke and to appoint gospel ordinances more rational and easy. He had indeed something more and greater in his view, in coming into the world, than merely to deliver us from the bondage of the ceremonial law; for he came in our nature, and consented to suffer and die for us, that hereby he might redeem us from the wrath of God, and from the curse of the moral law, which, as sinners, we all lay under. But that was one end of it, and a mercy reserved to be bestowed at the time of his manifestation; then the more servile state of the church was to come to a period, and a better to succeed in the place of it; for he was sent to redeem us, <hi type="italic">that we might receive the adoption of sons</hi>—that we might no longer be accounted and treated as servants, but as sons grown up to maturity, who are allowed greater freedoms, and admitted to larger privileges, than while they were under tutors and governors. This the course of the apostle's argument leads us to take notice of, as one thing intended by this expression, though no doubt it may also be understood as signifying that gracious adoption which the gospel so often speaks of as the privilege of those who believe in Christ. Israel was God's son, his first-born, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>. But now, under the gospel, particular believers receive the adoption; and, as an earnest and evidence of it, they have together therewith the Spirit of adoption, putting them upon the duty of prayer, and enabling them in prayer to eye God as a Father (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Because you are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying Abba, Father.</hi> And hereupon (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.7">v. 7</reference>) the apostle concludes this argument by adding, <hi type="italic">Wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and, if a son, then an heir of God through Christ;</hi> that is, Now, under the gospel state, we are no longer under the servitude of the law, but, upon our believing in Christ, become the sons of God; we are thereupon accepted of him, and adopted by him; and, being the sons, we are also heirs of God, and are entitled to the heavenly inheritance (as he also reasons <reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">Rom. viii. 17</reference>), and therefore it must needs be the greatest weakness and folly to turn back to the law, and to seek justification by the works of it. From what the apostle says in <reference osisRef="Gal.4.1-Gal.4.7">these verses</reference>, we may observe, <div eID="gen31729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31730" type="x-p"/> 1. The wonders of divine love and mercy towards us, particularly of God the Father, in sending his Son into the world to redeem and save us,—of the Son of God, in submitting so low, and suffering so much, for us, in pursuance of that design,—and of the Holy Spirit, in condescending to dwell in the hearts of believers for such gracious purposes. <div eID="gen31730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31731" type="x-p"/> 2. The great and invaluable advantages which Christians enjoy under the gospel; for, (1.) We receive <hi type="italic">the adoption of sons.</hi> Whence note, It is the great privilege which believers have through Christ that they are adopted children of the God of heaven. We who by nature are children of wrath and disobedience have become by grace children of love. (2.) We receive <hi type="italic">the Spirit of adoption.</hi> Note, [1.] All who have the privilege of adoption have the Spirit of adoption—all who are received into the number partake of the nature of the children of God; for he will have all his children to resemble him. [2.] The Spirit of adoption is always the Spirit of prayer, and it is our duty in prayer to eye God as a Father. Christ has taught us in prayer to eye God as our Father in heaven. [3.] If we are his sons, then his heirs. It is not so among men, with whom the eldest son is heir; but all God's children are heirs. Those who have the nature of sons shall have the inheritance of sons.
entries.38627d2ece0f660c31645107a2f41e83f8e4de4e: <div eID="gen31731" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Affectionate Remonstrance. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31732" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Howbeit then, when ye knew not God, ye did service unto them which by nature are no gods. <hi type="super">9</hi> But now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God, how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage? <hi type="super">10</hi> Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years. <hi type="super">11</hi> I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain. <div eID="gen31732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31733" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle puts them in mind of what they were before their conversion to the faith of Christ, and what a blessed change their conversion had made upon them; and thence endeavours to convince them of their great weakness in hearkening to those who would bring them under the bondage of the law of Moses. <div eID="gen31733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31734" type="x-p"/> I. He reminds them of their past state and behaviour, and what they were before the gospel was preached to them. Then <hi type="italic">they knew not God;</hi> they were grossly ignorant of the true God, and the way wherein he is to be worshipped: and at that time they were under the worst of slaveries, for <hi type="italic">they did service to those which by nature were no gods,</hi> they were employed in a great number of superstitious and idolatrous services to those who, though they were accounted gods, were yet really no gods, but mere creatures, and perhaps of their own making, and therefore were utterly unable to hear and help them. Note, 1. Those who are ignorant of the true God cannot but be inclined to false gods. Those who forsook the God who made the world, rather than be without gods, worshipped such as they themselves made. 2. Religious worship is due to none but to him who is by nature God; for, when the apostle blames the doing service to such as by nature were no gods, he plainly shows that he only who is by nature God is the proper object of our religious worship. <div eID="gen31734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31735" type="x-p"/> II. He calls upon them to consider the happy change that was made in them by the preaching of the gospel among them. Now <hi type="italic">they had known God</hi> (they were brought to the knowledge of the true God and of his Son Jesus Christ, whereby they were recovered out of the ignorance and bondage under which they before lay) <hi type="italic">or rather were known of God;</hi> this happy change in their state, whereby they were turned from idols to the living God, and through Christ had received the adoption of sons, was not owing to themselves, but to him; it was the effect of his free and rich grace towards them, and as such they ought to account it; and therefore hereby they were laid under the greater obligation to adhere to the liberty wherewith he had made them free. Note, All our acquaintance with God begins with him; we know him, because we are known of him. <div eID="gen31735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31736" type="x-p"/> III. Hence he infers the unreasonableness and madness of their suffering themselves to be brought again into a state of bondage. He speaks of it with surprise and deep concern of mind that such as they should do so: <hi type="italic">How turn you again,</hi> &c., says he, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">v. 9</reference>. "How is it that you, who have been taught to worship God in the gospel way, should not be persuaded to comply with the ceremonial way of worship? that you, who have been acquainted with a dispensation of light, liberty, and love, as that of the gospel is, should now submit to a dispensation of darkness, and bondage, and terror, as that of the law is?" This they had the less reason for, since they had never been under the law of Moses, as the Jews had been; and therefore on this account they were more inexcusable than the Jews themselves, who might be supposed to have some fondness for that which had been of such long standing among them. Besides, what they suffered themselves to be brought into bondage to were but <hi type="italic">weak and beggarly elements,</hi> such things as had no power in them to cleanse the soul, nor to afford any solid satisfaction to the mind, and which were only designed for that state of pupillage under which the church had been, but which had now come to a period; and therefore their weakness and folly were the more aggravated, in submitting to them, and in symbolizing with the Jews in observing their various festivals, here signified by <hi type="italic">days, and months, and times, and years.</hi> Here note, 1. It is possible for those who have made great professions of religion to be afterwards drawn into very great defections from the purity and simplicity of it, for this was the case of these Christians. And, 2. The more mercy God has shown to any, in bringing them into an acquaintance with the gospel, and the liberties and privileges of it, the greater are their sin and folly in suffering themselves to be deprived of them; for this the apostle lays a special stress upon, that after they had known God, or rather were known of him, they desired to be in bondage under the weak and beggarly elements of the law. <div eID="gen31736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31737" type="x-p"/> IV. Hereupon he expresses his fears concerning them, <hi type="italic">lest he had bestowed on them labour in vain.</hi> He had been at a great deal of pains about them, in preaching the gospel to them, and endeavouring to confirm them in the faith and liberty of it; but now they were giving up these, and thereby rendering his labour among them fruitless and ineffectual, and with the thoughts of this he could not but be deeply affected. Note, 1. A great deal of the labour of faithful ministers is labour in vain; and, when it is so, it cannot but be a great grief to those who desire the salvation of souls. Note, 2. The labour of ministers is in vain upon those who begin in the Spirit and end in the flesh, who, though they seem to set out well, yet afterwards turn aside from the way of the gospel. Note, 3. Those will have a great deal to answer for upon whom the faithful ministers of Jesus Christ bestow labour in vain.
entries.d466b8a5f6c1aa1104db284e41f0687c1ea44a55: <div eID="gen31737" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Affectionate Remonstrance. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31738" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Brethren, I beseech you, be as I <hi type="italic">am;</hi> for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> as ye <hi type="italic">are:</hi> ye have not injured me at all. 13 Ye know how through infirmity of the flesh I preached the gospel unto you at the first. <hi type="super">14</hi> And my temptation which was in my flesh ye despised not, nor rejected; but received me as an angel of God, <hi type="italic">even</hi> as Christ Jesus. <hi type="super">15</hi> Where is then the blessedness ye spake of? for I bear you record, that, if <hi type="italic">it had been</hi> possible, ye would have plucked out your own eyes, and have given them to me. <hi type="super">16</hi> Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth? <div eID="gen31738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31739" type="x-p"/> That these Christians might be the more ashamed of their defection from the truth of the gospel which Paul had preached to them, he here reminds them of the great affection they formerly had for him and his ministry, and puts them upon considering how very unsuitable their present behaviour was to what they then professed. And here we may observe, <div eID="gen31739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31740" type="x-p"/> I. How affectionately he addresses himself to them. He styles them brethren, though he knew their hearts were in a great measure alienated from him. He desires that all resentments might be laid aside, and that they would bear the same temper of mind towards him which he did to them; he would have them <hi type="italic">to be as he was, for he was as they were,</hi> and moreover tells them that <hi type="italic">they had not injured him at all.</hi> He had no quarrel with them upon his own account. Though, in blaming their conduct, he had expressed himself with some warmth and concern of mind he assured them that it was not owing to any sense of personal injury or affront (as they might be ready to think), but proceeded wholly from a zeal for the truth and purity of the gospel, and their welfare and happiness. Thus he endeavours to mollify their spirits towards him, that so they might be the better disposed to receive the admonitions he was giving them. Hereby he teaches us that in reproving others we should take care to convince them that our reproofs do not proceed from any private pique or resentment, but from a sincere regard to the honour of God and religion and their truest welfare; for they are then likely to be most successful when they appear to be most disinterested. <div eID="gen31740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31741" type="x-p"/> II. How he magnifies their former affection to him, that hereby they might be the more ashamed of their present behaviour towards him. To this purpose, 1. He puts them in mind of the difficulty under which he laboured when he came first among them: <hi type="italic">I knew,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">how, through infirmity of the flesh, I preached the gospel unto you at the first.</hi> What this <hi type="italic">infirmity of the flesh</hi> was, which in the following words he expresses by <hi type="italic">his temptation that was in his flesh</hi> (though, no doubt, it was well known to those Christians to whom he wrote), we can now have no certain knowledge of: some take it to have been the persecutions which he suffered for the gospel's sake; others, to have been something in his person, or manner of speaking, which might render his ministry less grateful and acceptable, referring to <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2 Cor. x. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7-2Cor.12.10">and to ch. xii. 7-10</reference>. But, whatever it was, it seems it made no impression on them to his disadvantage. For, 2. He takes notice that, notwithstanding this his infirmity (which might possibly lessen him in the esteem of some others), they did not despise nor reject him on the account of it, but, on the contrary, <hi type="italic">received him as an angel of God, even as Christ Jesus.</hi> They showed a great deal of respect to him, he was a welcome messenger to them, even as though an angel of God or Jesus Christ himself had preached to them; yea, so great was their esteem of him, that, if it would have been any advantage to him, <hi type="italic">they could have plucked out their own eyes, and have given them to him.</hi> Note, How uncertain the respects of people are, how apt they are to change their minds, and how easily they are drawn into contempt of those for whom they once had the greatest esteem and affection, so that they are ready to pluck out the eyes of those for whom they would before have plucked out their own! We should therefore labour to be accepted of God, <hi type="italic">for it is a small thing to be judged of man's judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.2">1 Cor. iv. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen31741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31742" type="x-p"/> III. How earnestly he expostulates with them hereupon: <hi type="italic">Where is then,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">the blessedness you spoke of?</hi> As if he had said, "Time was when you expressed the greatest joy and satisfaction in the glad tidings of the gospel, and were very forward in pouring out your blessings upon me as the publisher of them; whence is it that you are now so much altered, that you have so little relish of them or respect for me? You once thought yourselves happy in receiving the gospel; have you now any reason to think otherwise?" Note, Those who have left their first love would do well to consider, Where is now the blessedness they once spoke of? What has become of that pleasure they used to take in communion with God, and in the company of his servants? The more to impress upon them a just shame of their present conduct, he again asks (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.16">v. 16</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Am I become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?</hi> How is it that I, who was heretofore your favourite, am now accounted your enemy? Can you pretend any other reason for it than that I have told you the truth, endeavoured to acquaint you with, and to confirm you in, the truth of the gospel? And, if not, how unreasonable must your disaffection be!" Note, 1. It is no uncommon thing for men to account those their enemies who are really their best friends; for so, undoubtedly, those are, whether ministers or others, who tell them the truth, and deal freely and faithfully with them in matters relating to their eternal salvation, as the apostle now did with these Christians. 2. Ministers may sometimes create enemies to themselves by the faithful discharge of their duty; for this was the case of Paul, he was accounted their enemy for telling them the truth. 3. Yet ministers must not forbear speaking the truth, for fear of offending others and drawing their displeasure upon them. 4. They may be easy in their own minds, when they are conscious to themselves that, if others have become their enemies, it is only for telling them the truth.
entries.6ad92ce2a90f689d750ca7e3a57e74df1d39e6d5: <div eID="gen31742" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Affectionate Remonstrance. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31743" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> They zealously affect you, <hi type="italic">but</hi> not well; yea, they would exclude you, that ye might affect them. 18 But <hi type="italic">it is</hi> good to be zealously affected always in <hi type="italic">a</hi> good <hi type="italic">thing,</hi> and not only when I am present with you. <div eID="gen31743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31744" type="x-p"/> The apostle is still carrying on the same design as in the <reference osisRef="Gal.4.12-Gal.4.16">foregoing verses</reference>, which was, to convince the Galatians of their sin and folly in departing from the truth of the gospel: having just before been expostulating with them about the change of their behaviour towards him who endeavoured to establish them in it, he here gives them the character of those false teachers who made it their business to draw them away from it, which if they would attend to, they might soon see how little reason they had to hearken to them: whatever opinion they might have of them, he tells them they were designing men, who were aiming to set up themselves, and who, under their specious pretences, were more consulting their own interest than theirs: "<hi type="italic">They zealously affect you,</hi>" says he; "they show a mighty respect for you, and pretend a great deal of affection to you, <hi type="italic">but not well;</hi> they do it not with any good design, they are not sincere and upright in it, for <hi type="italic">they would exclude you, that you might affect them.</hi> That which they are chiefly aiming at is to engage your affections to them; and, in order to this, they are doing all they can to draw off your affections from me and from the truth, that so they may engross you to themselves." This, he assures them, was their design, and therefore they must needs be very unwise in hearkening to them. Note, 1. There may appear to be a great deal of zeal where yet there is but little truth and sincerity. 2. It is the usual way of seducers to insinuate themselves into people's affections, and by that means to draw them into their opinions. 3. Whatever pretences such may make, they have usually more regard to their own interest than that of others, and will not stick at ruining the reputation of others, if by that means they can raise their own. On this occasion the apostle gives us that excellent rule which we have, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.18">v. 18</reference>, <hi type="italic">It is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing.</hi> What our translation renders <hi type="italic">in a good man,</hi> and so consider the apostle as pointing to himself; this sense, they think, is favoured both by the preceding context and also by the words immediately following, <hi type="italic">and not only when I am present with you,</hi> which may be as if he had said, "Time was when you were zealously affected towards me; you once took me for a good man, and have now no reason to think otherwise of me; surely then it would become you to show the same regard to me, now that I am absent from you, which you did when I was present with you." But, if we adhere to our own translation, the apostle here furnishes us with a very good rule to direct and regulate us in the exercise of our zeal: there are two things which to this purpose he more especially recommends to us:— (1.) That it be exercised only upon that which is good; for zeal is then only good when it is in a good thing: those who are zealously affected to that which is evil will thereby only to do so much the more hurt. And, (2.) That herein it be constant and steady: it is good to be zealous always in a good thing; not for a time only, or now and then, like the heat of an ague-fit, but, like the natural heat of the body, constant. Happy would it be for the church of Christ if this rule were better observed among Christians!
entries.80b959523bf1103dca7fed84e4090bc288ab7e56: <div eID="gen31744" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Affectionate Remonstrance. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31745" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you, <hi type="super">20</hi> I desire to be present with you now, and to change my voice; for I stand in doubt of you. <div eID="gen31745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31746" type="x-p"/> That the apostle might the better dispose these Christians to bear with him in the reproofs which he was obliged to give them, he here expresses his great affection to them, and the very tender concern he had for their welfare: he was not like them—one thing when among them and another when absent from them. Their disaffection to him had not removed his affection from them; but he still bore the same respect to them which he had formerly done, nor was he like their false teachers, who pretended a great deal of affection to them, when at the same time they were only consulting their own interest; but he had a sincere concern for their truest advantage; he sought not theirs, but them. They were too ready to account him their enemy, but he assures them that he was their friend; nay, not only so, but that he had the bowels of a parent towards them. He calls them <hi type="italic">his children,</hi> as he justly might, since he had been the instrument of their conversion to the Christian faith; yea, he styles them his <hi type="italic">little children,</hi> which, as it denotes a greater degree of tenderness and affection to them, so it may possibly have a respect to their present behaviour, whereby they showed themselves too much like little children, who are easily wrought upon by the arts and insinuations of others. He expresses his concern for them, and earnest desire of their welfare and soul-prosperity, by the pangs of a travailing woman: <hi type="italic">He travailed in birth for them:</hi> and the great thing which he was in so much pain about, and which he was so earnestly desirous of, was not so much that they might affect him as <hi type="italic">that Christ might be formed in them,</hi> that they might become Christians indeed, and be more confirmed and established in the faith of the gospel. From this we may note, 1. The very tender affection which faithful ministers bear towards those among whom they are employed; it is like that of the most affectionate parents to their little children. 2. That the chief thing they are longing and even travailing in birth for, on their account, is that Christ may be formed in them; not so much that they may gain their affections, much less that they may make a prey of them, but that they may be renewed in the spirit of their minds, wrought into the image of Christ, and more fully settled and confirmed in the Christian faith and life: and how unreasonably must those people act who suffer themselves to be prevailed upon to desert or dislike such ministers! 3. That Christ is not fully formed in men till they are brought off from trusting in their own righteousness, and made to rely only upon him and his righteousness. <div eID="gen31746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31747" type="x-p"/> As further evidence of the affection and concern which the apostle had for these Christians, he adds (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.20">v. 20</reference>) that <hi type="italic">he desired to be then present with them</hi>—that he would be glad of an opportunity of being among them, and conversing with them, and that thereupon he might find occasion <hi type="italic">to change his voice</hi> towards them; for at present <hi type="italic">he stood in doubt of them.</hi> He knew not well what to think of them. He was not so fully acquainted with their state as to know how to accommodate himself to them. He was full of fears and jealousies concerning them, which was the reason of his writing to them in such a manner as he had done; but he would be glad to find that matters were better with them than he feared, and that he might have occasion to commend them, instead of thus reproving and chiding them. Note, Though ministers too often find it necessary to reprove those they have to do with, yet this is no grateful work to them; they had much rather there were no occasion for it, and are always glad when they can see reason to change their voice towards them.
entries.c116b8d0f4fcac89ff6ad42581fbfc7066d649d5: <div eID="gen31747" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Affectionate Remonstrance. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 56.)</title> <div sID="gen31748" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Tell me, ye that desire to be under the law, do ye not hear the law? <hi type="super">22</hi> For it is written, that Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman. 23 But he <hi type="italic">who was</hi> of the bondwoman was born after the flesh; but he of the freewoman <hi type="italic">was</hi> by promise. <hi type="super">24</hi> Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants; the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar. <hi type="super">25</hi> For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia, and answereth to Jerusalem which now is, and is in bondage with her children. <hi type="super">26</hi> But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all. <hi type="super">27</hi> For it is written, Rejoice, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> barren that bearest not; break forth and cry, thou that travailest not: for the desolate hath many more children than she which hath a husband. <hi type="super">28</hi> Now we, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of promise. <hi type="super">29</hi> But as then he that was born after the flesh persecuted him <hi type="italic">that was born</hi> after the Spirit, even so <hi type="italic">it is</hi> now. <hi type="super">30</hi> Nevertheless what saith the scripture? Cast out the bondwoman and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman. 31 So then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free. <div eID="gen31748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31749" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle illustrates the difference between believers who rested in Christ only and those judaizers who trusted in the law, by a comparison taken from the story of Isaac and Ishmael. This he introduces in such a manner as was proper to strike and impress their minds, and to convince them of their great weakness in departing from the truth, and suffering themselves to be deprived of the liberty of the gospel: <hi type="italic">Tell me,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">you that desire to be under the law, do you not hear the law?</hi> He takes it for granted that they did hear the law, for among the Jews it was wont to be read in their public assemblies every sabbath day; and, since they were so very fond of being under it, he would have them duly to consider what is written therein (referring to what is recorded <reference osisRef="Gen.16.1-Gen.16.16">Gen. xvi.</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.21.1-Gen.21.34">xxi.</reference>), for, if they would do this, they might soon see how little reason they had to trust in it. And here, 1. He sets before them the history itself (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.22-Gal.4.23">v. 22, 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">For it is written, Abraham had two sons,</hi> &c. Here he represents the different state and condition of these two sons of Abraham—that the one, Ishmael, <hi type="italic">was by a bond-maid,</hi> and the other, Isaac, <hi type="italic">by a free-woman;</hi> and that whereas the former <hi type="italic">was born after the flesh,</hi> or by the ordinary course of nature, the other <hi type="italic">was by promise,</hi> when in the course of nature there was no reason to expect that Sarah should have a son. 2. He acquaints them with the meaning and design of this history, or the use which he intended to make of it (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.24-Gal.4.27">v. 24-27</reference>): <hi type="italic">These things,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">are an allegory,</hi> wherein, besides the literal and historical sense of the words, the Spirit of God might design to signify something further to us, and that was, That these two, Agar and Sarah, <hi type="italic">are the two covenants,</hi> or were intended to typify and prefigure the two different dispensations of the covenant. The former, Agar, represented that which was given from mount Sinai, and <hi type="italic">which gendereth to bondage,</hi> which, though it was a dispensation of grace, yet, in comparison of the gospel state, was a dispensation of bondage, and became more so to the Jews, through their mistake of the design of it, and expecting to be justified by the works of it. <hi type="italic">For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia</hi> (mount Sinai was then called Agar by the Arabians), <hi type="italic">and it answereth to Jerusalem which now is, and is in bondage with her children;</hi> that is, it justly represents the present state of the Jews, who, continuing in their infidelity and adhering to that covenant, are still in bondage with their children. But the other, Sarah, was intended to prefigure Jerusalem which is above, or the state of Christians under the new and better dispensation of the covenant, which is free both from the curse of the moral and the bondage of the ceremonial law, and <hi type="italic">is the mother of us all</hi>—a state into which all, both Jews and Gentiles, are admitted, upon their believing in Christ. And to this greater freedom and enlargement of the church under the gospel dispensation, which was typified by Sarah the mother of the promised seed, the apostle refers that of the prophet, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa. liv. 1</reference>, where it is written, <hi type="italic">Rejoice, thou barren that bearest not; break forth and cry, thou that travailest not; for the desolate hath many more children than she who hath a husband.</hi> 3. He applies the history thus explained to the present case (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.28">v. 28</reference>); <hi type="italic">Now we, brethren,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">as Isaac was, are the children of the promise.</hi> We Christians, who have accepted Christ, and rely upon him, and look for justification and salvation by him alone, as hereby we become the spiritual, though we are not the natural, seed of Abraham, so we are entitled to the promised inheritance and interested in the blessings of it. But lest these Christians should be stumbled at the opposition they might meet with from the Jews, who were so tenacious of their law as to be ready to persecute those who would not submit to it, he tells them that this was no more than what was pointed to in the type; for <hi type="italic">as then he that was born after the flesh persecuted him that was born after the Spirit,</hi> they must expect it would be <hi type="italic">so now.</hi> But, for their comfort in this case, he desires them to consider what the scripture saith (<reference osisRef="Gen.21.10">Gen. xxi. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">Cast out the bond-woman and her son, for the son of the bond-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free-woman.</hi> Though the judaizers should persecute and hate them, yet the issue would be that Judaism would sink, and wither, and perish; but true Christianity should flourish and last for ever. And then, as a general inference from the whole of the sum of what he had said, he concludes (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.31">v. 31</reference>), <hi type="italic">So then, brethren, we are not children of the bond-woman, but of the free.</hi>  <chapter eID="Gal.4"/> <div eID="gen31749" type="x-p"/>

entries.2844560e251636b26396db01be10ac02d09f21cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17496"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gal.4.1-Gal.4.31">Ga 4:1-31</reference>. The Same Subject Continued: Illustration of Our Subjection to the Law Only till Christ Came, from the Subjection of an Heir to His Guardian till He Is of Age. Peter's Good Will to the Galatians Should Lead Them to the Same Good Will to Him as They Had at First Shown. Their Desire to Be under the Law Shown by the Allegory of Isaac and Ishmael to Be Inconsistent with Their Gospel Liberty.</title> <div sID="gen35105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17496"/>1-7. The fact of God's sending His Son to redeem us who were under the law (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">Ga 4:4</reference>), and sending the Spirit of His Son into our hearts (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Ga 4:6</reference>), confirms the conclusion (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.29">Ga 3:29</reference>) that we are "heirs according to the promise."<div eID="gen35105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the heir--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gal.3.29">Ga 3:29</reference>). It is not, as in earthly inheritances, the death of the father, but our Father's sovereign will simply that makes us heirs.<div eID="gen35106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">child--</hi>Greek, "one under age."<div eID="gen35107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">differeth nothing, &c.--</hi>that is, has no more freedom than a slave (so the Greek for "servant" means). He is not at his own disposal.<div eID="gen35108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lord of all--</hi>by title and virtual ownership (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21">1Co 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22">22</reference>). <div eID="gen35109" type="x-p"/>
entries.72ef04bda86e7d7b559ae9505763d7f4c9246229: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17503"/><div sID="gen35132" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17503"/>8-11. Appeal to them not to turn back from their privileges as free sons, to legal bondage again.<div eID="gen35132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>when ye were "servants" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.7">Ga 4:7</reference>).<div eID="gen35133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye knew not God--</hi>not opposed to <reference osisRef="Rom.1.21">Ro 1:21</reference>. The heathen originally knew God, as <reference osisRef="Rom.1.21">Ro 1:21</reference> states, but did not choose to retain God in their knowledge, and so corrupted the original truth. They might still have known Him, in a measure, from His works, but as a matter of fact they knew Him not, so far as His eternity, His power as the Creator, and His holiness, are concerned.<div eID="gen35134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are no gods--</hi>that is, have no existence, such as their worshippers attribute to them, in the nature of things, but only in the corrupt imaginations of their worshippers (see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.4">1Co 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.19">1Co 10:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.9">2Ch 13:9</reference>). Your "service" was a different bondage from that of the Jews, which was a true service. Yet theirs, like yours, was a burdensome yoke; how then is it ye wish to resume the yoke after that God has transferred both Jews and Gentiles to a free service? <div eID="gen35135" type="x-p"/>
entries.90c3d6ac85d102b978f7fa983116ef07689a7307: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17507"/><div sID="gen35147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17507"/><hi type="bold">12. be as I am--</hi>"As I have in my life among you cast off Jewish habits, so do ye; for I am become as ye are," namely, in the non-observance of legal ordinances. "The fact of my laying them aside among Gentiles, shows that I regard them as not at all contributing to justification or sanctification. Do you regard them in the same light, and act accordingly." His observing the law among the Jews was not inconsistent with this, for he did so only in order to win them, without compromising principle. On the other hand, the Galatian Gentiles, by adopting legal ordinances, showed that they regarded them as needful for salvation. This Paul combats.<div eID="gen35147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye have not injured me at all--</hi>namely, at the period when I first preached the Gospel among you, and when I made myself as you are, namely, living as a Gentile, not as a Jew. You at that time did me no wrong; "ye did not despise my temptation in the flesh" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.14">Ga 4:14</reference>): nay, you "received me as an angel of God." Then in <reference osisRef="Gal.4.16">Ga 4:16</reference>, he asks, "Have I then, since that time, become your enemy by telling you the truth?" <div eID="gen35148" type="x-p"/>
entries.46a24acd1777cf9256d3beed19a9a9191891f0c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17508"/><div sID="gen35149" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17508"/><hi type="bold">13. how through infirmity--</hi>rather, as Greek, "Ye know that because of an infirmity of my flesh I preached," &c. He implies that bodily sickness, having detained him among them, contrary to his original intentions, was the occasion of his preaching the Gospel to them.<div eID="gen35149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35150" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the first--</hi>literally, "at the former time"; implying that at the time of writing he had been twice in Galatia. See my Introduction; also see on <reference osisRef="Gal.4.16">Ga 4:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Gal.5.21">Ga 5:21</reference>. His sickness was probably the same as recurred more violently afterward, "the thorn in the flesh" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:7</reference>), which also was overruled to good (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">2Co 12:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">10</reference>), as the "infirmity of the flesh" here. <div eID="gen35150" type="x-p"/>
entries.c09fc1fbcf8610796aa272ead9a540fea29e10cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17509"/><div sID="gen35151" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17509"/><hi type="bold">14. my temptation--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "your temptation." My infirmity, which was, or might have been, a "temptation," or trial, to you, ye despised not, that is, ye were not tempted by it to despise me and my message. Perhaps, however, it is better to punctuate and explain as Lachmann, connecting it with <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>, "And (ye know) your temptation (that is, the temptation to which ye were exposed through the infirmity) which was in my flesh. Ye despised not (through natural pride), nor rejected (through spiritual pride), but received me," &c. "Temptation does not mean here, as we now use the word, tendency to an evil habit, but BODILY TRIAL."<div eID="gen35151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as an angel of God--</hi>as a heaven-inspired and sent messenger from God: angel means "messenger" (Mal 2:7). Compare the phrase, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.27">2Sa 19:27</reference>, a Hebrew and Oriental one for a person to be received with the highest respect (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.8">Zec 12:8</reference>). An angel is free from the flesh, infirmity, and temptation.<div eID="gen35152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as Christ--</hi>being Christ's representative (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.40">Mt 10:40</reference>). Christ is Lord of angels. <div eID="gen35153" type="x-p"/>
entries.f06aadfe99423c0c1d46c30e5fa4ec6aebf5bff2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17510"/><div sID="gen35154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17510"/><hi type="bold">15. Where, &c.--</hi>Of what value was your congratulation (so the Greek for "blessedness" expresses) of yourselves, on account of your having among you me, the messenger of the Gospel, considering how entirely you have veered about since? Once you counted yourselves blessed in being favored with my ministry.<div eID="gen35154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye would have plucked out your own eyes--</hi>one of the dearest members of the body--so highly did you value me: a proverbial phrase for the greatest self-sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.29">Mt 5:29</reference>). Conybeare and Howson think that this particular form of proverb was used with reference to a weakness in Paul's eyes, connected with a nervous frame, perhaps affected by the brightness of the vision described, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.11">Ac 22:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1-2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:1-7</reference>. "You would have torn out your own eyes to supply the lack of mine." The divine power of Paul's words and works, contrasting with the feebleness of his person (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2Co 10:10</reference>), powerfully at first impressed the Galatians, who had all the impulsiveness of the Celtic race from which they sprang. Subsequently they soon changed with the fickleness which is equally characteristic of Celts. <div eID="gen35155" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab47e34e45905dc9e05ad2d1f988875639e8abcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17511"/><div sID="gen35156" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17511"/>16. Translate, "Am I then become your enemy (an enemy in your eyes) by telling you the truth" (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.5">Ga 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">14</reference>)? He plainly did not incur their enmity at his first visit, and the words here imply that he had since then, and before his now writing, incurred it: so that the occasion of his telling them the unwelcome truth, must have been at his second visit (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.23">Ac 18:23</reference>, see my Introduction). The fool and sinner hate a reprover. The righteous love faithful reproof (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Psa 141:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.9.8">Pr 9:8</reference>). <div eID="gen35156" type="x-p"/>
entries.35599bbc339065521d878d11f53f9489b5fe49d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17512"/><div sID="gen35157" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17512"/><hi type="bold">17. They--</hi>your flatterers: in contrast to Paul himself, who tells them the truth.<div eID="gen35157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">zealously--</hi>zeal in proselytism was characteristic especially of the Jews, and so of Judaizers (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.14">Ga 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.15">Mt 23:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.2">Ro 10:2</reference>).<div eID="gen35158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">affect you--</hi>that is, court you (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Co 11:2</reference>).<div eID="gen35159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not well--</hi>not in a good way, or for a good end. Neither the cause of their zealous courting of you, nor the manner, is what it ought to be.<div eID="gen35160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they would exclude you--</hi>"They wish to shut you out" from the kingdom of God (that is, they wish to persuade you that as uncircumcised Gentiles, you are shut out from it), "that ye may zealously court them," that is, become circumcised, as zealous followers of themselves. Alford explains it, that their wish was to shut out the Galatians from the general community, and attract them as a separate clique to their own party. So the English word "exclusive," is used. <div eID="gen35161" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5350289539ec4be2daf42cc206c33c7b39c37f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17513"/><div sID="gen35162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17513"/><hi type="bold">18. good to be zealously affected--</hi>rather, to correspond to "zealously court" in <reference osisRef="Gal.4.18">Ga 4:18</reference>, "to be zealously courted." I do not find fault with them for zealously courting you, nor with you for being zealously courted: provided it be "in a good cause" (translate so), "it is a good thing" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.20-1Cor.9.23">1Co 9:20-23</reference>). My reason for saying the "not well" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.17">Ga 4:17</reference>; the Greek is the same as that for "good," and "in a good cause," in <reference osisRef="Gal.4.28">Ga 4:28</reference>), is that their zealous courting of you is not in a good cause. The older interpreters, however, support English Version (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.14">Ga 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen35162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">always--</hi>Translate and arrange the words thus, "At all times, and not only when I am present with you." I do not desire that I exclusively should have the privilege of zealously courting you. Others may do so in my absence with my full approval, if only it be in a good cause, and if Christ be faithfully preached (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.15-Phil.1.18">Php 1:15-18</reference>). <div eID="gen35163" type="x-p"/>
entries.8794d0dc5a2a7f986eabf4ee272c686f7f008357: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17514"/><div sID="gen35164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17514"/><hi type="bold">19. My little children--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.1">2Ti 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1Jo 2:1</reference>). My relation to you is not merely that of one zealously courting you (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.17">Ga 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.18">18</reference>), but that of a father to his children (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">1Co 4:15</reference>).<div eID="gen35164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I travail in birth--</hi>that is, like a mother in pain till the birth of her child.<div eID="gen35165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">again--</hi>a second time. The former time was when I was "present with you" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.18">Ga 4:18</reference>; compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen35166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Christ be formed in you--</hi>that you may live nothing but Christ, and think nothing but Christ (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>), and glory in nothing but Him, and His death, resurrection, and righteousness (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.8-Phil.3.10">Php 3:8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col 1:27</reference>). <div eID="gen35167" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3421dc1a21be838db393215c438f775eb57a659: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17515"/><div sID="gen35168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17515"/>20. Translate as Greek, "I could wish." If circumstances permitted (which they do not), I would gladly be with you [M. Stuart].<div eID="gen35168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>as I was twice already. Speaking face to face is so much more effective towards loving persuasion than writing (2Jo 12; 3Jo 13, 14).<div eID="gen35169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">change my voice--</hi>as a mother (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.19">Ga 4:19</reference>): adapting my tone of voice to what I saw in person your case might need. This is possible to one present, but not to one in writing [Grotius and Estius].<div eID="gen35170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I stand in doubt of you--</hi>rather, "I am perplexed about you," namely, how to deal with you, what kind of words to use, gentle or severe, to bring you back to the right path. <div eID="gen35171" type="x-p"/>
entries.156af513251272b6b1948a7637562f4165fff31f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17516"/><div sID="gen35172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17516"/><hi type="bold">21. desire--</hi>of your own accord madly courting that which must condemn and ruin you.<div eID="gen35172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do ye not hear--</hi>do ye not consider the mystic sense of Moses' words? [Grotius]. The law itself sends you away from itself to Christ [Estius]. After having sufficiently maintained his point by argument, the apostle confirms and illustrates it by an inspired allegorical exposition of historical facts, containing in them general laws and types. Perhaps his reason for using allegory was to confute the Judaizers with their own weapons: subtle, mystical, allegorical interpretations, unauthorized by the Spirit, were their favorite arguments, as of the Rabbins in the synagogues. Compare the Jerusalem Talmud [Tractatu Succa, cap. Hechalil]. Paul meets them with an allegorical exposition, not the work of fancy, but sanctioned by the Holy Spirit. History, if properly understood contains in its complicated phenomena, simple and continually recurring divine laws. The history of the elect people, like their legal ordinances, had, besides the literal, a typical meaning (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1-1Cor.4.15">1Co 10:1-4; 15</reference>:45, 47; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.8">Re 11:8</reference>). Just as the extra-ordinarily-born Isaac, the gift of grace according to promise, supplanted, beyond all human calculations, the naturally-born Ishmael, so the new theocratic race, the spiritual seed of Abraham by promise, the Gentile, as well as Jewish believers, were about to take the place of the natural seed, who had imagined that to them exclusively belonged the kingdom of God. <div eID="gen35173" type="x-p"/>
entries.56e53aad03f99abb40f7c8e56eb06d91f3224a68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17517"/><div sID="gen35174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17517"/>22. (Ge 16:3-16; 21:2).<div eID="gen35174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Abraham--</hi>whose sons ye wish to be (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.9.7-Rom.9.9">Ro 9:7-9</reference>).<div eID="gen35175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a bond maid ... a free woman--</hi>rather, as Greek, "the bond maid ... the free woman." <div eID="gen35176" type="x-p"/>
entries.78dd4e252ba4348eaa53d2cb6e8c24b973e9a1cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17518"/><div sID="gen35177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17518"/><hi type="bold">23. after the flesh--</hi>born according to the usual course of nature: in contrast to Isaac, who was born "by virtue of the promise" (so the Greek), as the efficient cause of Sarah's becoming pregnant out of the course of nature (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.19">Ro 4:19</reference>). Abraham was to lay aside all confidence in the flesh (after which Ishmael was born), and to live by faith alone in the promise (according to which Isaac was miraculously born, contrary to all calculations of flesh and blood). <div eID="gen35177" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d1a00534107fe601c50c08bd183b4fde23b534b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17519"/><div sID="gen35178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17519"/><hi type="bold">24. are an allegory--</hi>rather, "are allegorical," that is, have another besides the literal meaning.<div eID="gen35178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these are the two covenants--</hi>"these [women] are (that is, mean; omit 'the' with all the oldest manuscripts) two covenants." As among the Jews the bondage of the mother determined that of the child, the children of the free covenant of promise, answering to Sarah, are free; the children of the legal covenant of bondage are not so.<div eID="gen35179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one from--</hi>that is, taking his origin from Mount Sinai. Hence, it appears, he is treating of the moral law (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Ga 3:19</reference>) chiefly (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">He 12:18</reference>). Paul was familiar with the district of Sinai in Arabia (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.17">Ga 1:17</reference>), having gone thither after his conversion. At the gloomy scene of the giving of the Law, he learned to appreciate, by contrast, the grace of the Gospel, and so to cast off all his past legal dependencies.<div eID="gen35180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which gendereth--</hi>that is, bringing forth children unto bondage. Compare the phrase (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.25">Ac 3:25</reference>), "children of the covenant which God made ... saying unto Abraham."<div eID="gen35181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Agar--</hi>that is, Hagar. <div eID="gen35182" type="x-p"/>
entries.67ce67c43b8328d3181cec8a947888e3af81f979: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17520"/><div sID="gen35183" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17520"/><hi type="bold">25. Translate, "For this word, Hagar, is (imports) Mount Sinai in Arabia (that is, among the Arabians--</hi>in the Arabian tongue)." So Chrysostom explains. Haraut, the traveller, says that to this day the Arabians call Sinai, "Hadschar," that is, Hagar, meaning a rock or stone. Hagar twice fled into the desert of Arabia (Ge 16:1-16; 21:9-21): from her the mountain and city took its name, and the people were called Hagarenes. Sinai, with its rugged rocks, far removed from the promised land, was well suited to represent the law which inspires with terror, and the spirit of bondage.<div eID="gen35183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">answereth--</hi>literally, "stands in the same rank with"; "she corresponds to."<div eID="gen35184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem which now is--</hi>that is, the Jerusalem of the Jews, having only a present temporary existence, in contrast with the spiritual Jerusalem of the Gospel, which in germ, under the form of the promise, existed ages before, and shall be for ever in ages to come.<div eID="gen35185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "For she is in bondage." As Hagar was in bondage to her mistress, so Jerusalem that now is, is in bondage to the law, and also to the Romans: her civil state thus being in accordance with her spiritual state [Bengel]. <div eID="gen35186" type="x-p"/>
entries.6dcd73bf888b8f43ba547cbe9d7c1ef78ce32f85: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17521"/><div sID="gen35187" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17521"/>26. This verse stands instead of the sentence which we should expect, to correspond to <reference osisRef="Gal.4.24">Ga 4:24</reference>, "One from Mount Sinai," namely, the other covenant from the heavenly mount above, which is (answers in the allegory to) Sarah.<div eID="gen35187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem ... above--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>), "the heavenly Jerusalem." "New Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God" (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Re 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">21:2</reference>). Here "the Messianic theocracy, which before Christ's second appearing is the Church, and after it, Christ's kingdom of glory" [Meyer].<div eID="gen35188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">free--</hi>as Sarah was; opposed to "she is in bondage" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.25">Ga 4:25</reference>).<div eID="gen35189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>omitted in many of the oldest manuscripts, though supported by some. "Mother of us," namely, believers who are already members of the invisible Church, the heavenly Jerusalem, hereafter to be manifested (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>). <div eID="gen35190" type="x-p"/>
entries.175b351238c142af7973dc03df622f3a6902c33d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17522"/><div sID="gen35191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17522"/>27. (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Is 54:1</reference>).<div eID="gen35191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou barren--</hi>Jerusalem above: the spiritual Church of the Gospel, the fruit of "the promise," answering to Sarah, who bore not "after the flesh": as contrasted with the law, answering to Hagar, who was fruitful in the ordinary course of nature. Isaiah speaks primarily of Israel's restoration after her long-continued calamities; but his language is framed by the Holy Spirit so as to reach beyond this to the spiritual Zion: including not only the Jews, the natural descendants of Abraham and children of the law, but also the Gentiles. The spiritual Jerusalem is regarded as "barren" while the law trammeled Israel, for she then had no spiritual children of the Gentiles.<div eID="gen35192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">break forth--</hi>into crying.<div eID="gen35193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cry--</hi>shout for joy.<div eID="gen35194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">many more--</hi>Translate as Greek, "Many are the children of the desolate (the New Testament Church made up in the greater part from the Gentiles, who once had not the promise, and so was destitute of God as her husband), more than of her which hath an (Greek, 'THE') husband (the Jewish Church having God for her husband, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jr 2:2</reference>)." Numerous as were the children of the legal covenant, those of the Gospel covenant are more so. The force of the Greek article is, "Her who has THE husband of which the other is destitute." <div eID="gen35195" type="x-p"/>
entries.521d997482eabd11d0121f2d321134820ecf2212: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17523"/><div sID="gen35196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17523"/><hi type="bold">28. we--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and versions are divided between "we" and "ye." "We" better accords with <reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">Ga 4:26</reference>, "mother of us."<div eID="gen35196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35197" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children of promise--</hi>not children after the flesh, but through the promise (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.23">Ga 4:23</reference>, 29, 31). "We are" so, and ought to wish to continue so. <div eID="gen35197" type="x-p"/>
entries.41d2f182be870769f21416132f765acc26e90ee0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17524"/><div sID="gen35198" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17524"/><hi type="bold">29. persecuted--</hi>Ishmael "mocked" Isaac, which contained in it the germ and spirit of persecution (<reference osisRef="Gen.21.9">Ge 21:9</reference>). His mocking was probably directed against Isaac's piety and faith in God's promises. Being the older by natural birth, he haughtily prided himself above him that was born by promise: as Cain hated Abel's piety.<div eID="gen35198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35199" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him ... born after the Spirit--</hi>The language, though referring primarily to Isaac, born in a spiritual way (namely, by the promise or word of God, rendered by His Spirit efficient out of the course of nature, in making Sarah fruitful in old age), is so framed as especially to refer to believers justified by Gospel grace through faith, as opposed to carnal men, Judaizers, and legalists.<div eID="gen35199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even so it is now--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gal.5.11">Ga 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.12">6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.29">Ac 9:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.45">13:45</reference>, 49, 50; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.1">14:1</reference>, 2, 19; 17:5, 13; 18:5, 6). The Jews persecuted Paul, not for preaching Christianity in opposition to heathenism, but for preaching it as distinct from Judaism. Except in the two cases of Philippi and Ephesus (where the persons beginning the assault were pecuniarily interested in his expulsion), he was nowhere set upon by the Gentiles, unless they were first stirred up by the Jews. The coincidence between Paul's Epistles and Luke's history (the Acts) in this respect, is plainly undesigned, and so a proof of genuineness (see Paley, Horæ Paulinæ). <div eID="gen35200" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a149d8037cbfe13ba0597e87a26885dec722047: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17525"/><div sID="gen35201" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17525"/>30. <reference osisRef="Gen.21.10">Ge 21:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.12">12</reference>, where Sarah's words are, "shall not be heir with my son, even with Isaac." But what was there said literally, is here by inspiration expressed in its allegorical spiritual import, applying to the New Testament believer, who is antitypically "the son of the free woman." In <reference osisRef="John.8.35">Joh 8:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.8.36">36</reference>, Jesus refers to this.<div eID="gen35201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Cast out--</hi>from the house and inheritance: literally, Ishmael; spiritually, the carnal and legalists.<div eID="gen35202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35203" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall not be heir--</hi>The Greek is stronger, "must not be heir," or "inherit." <div eID="gen35203" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b1e17518998405bebb7b35f780480d8bc2a534c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17526"/><div sID="gen35204" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17526"/><hi type="bold">31. So then--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "Wherefore." This is the conclusion inferred from what precedes. In <reference osisRef="Gal.3.29">Ga 3:29</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gal.4.7">Ga 4:7</reference>, it was established that we, New Testament believers, are "heirs." If, then, we are heirs, "we are not children of the bond woman (whose son, according to Scripture, was 'not to be heir,' <reference osisRef="Gal.4.30">Ga 4:30</reference>), but of the free woman (whose son was, according to Scripture, to be heir). For we are not "cast out" as Ishmael, but accepted as sons and heirs. <chapter eID="Gal.4"/>

entries.d83554c954842e4242a6f2616f4d13240c762d1f: <div eID="gen49728" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen49729" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen49730" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen49730" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen49729" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen49731" type="x-p"/> The apostle shows that, as an heir in nonage is under tutors and guardians, so were the Galatians while under the law; and, as the heir when he comes of age is no longer under guardians, so they, when the Gospel came, arrived at full maturity, and were redeemed from the law, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.1-Gal.4.3">Gal 4:1-3</reference>. He shows, farther, that when the fullness of the time came God sent forth his Son, that we might obtain the adoption of sons, and have the strongest evidence of that adoption, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.4-Gal.4.6">Gal 4:4-6</reference>. Those who are children of God are heirs of heaven, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.7">Gal 4:7</reference>. He compares their former and latter state, and shows the reason he had to fear that his labor on their behalf was in vain, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.8-Gal.4.11">Gal 4:8-11</reference>. He mentions his trials among them, and their kindness to him, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.12-Gal.4.16">Gal 4:12-16</reference>. Shows his tender affection for them, and exhorts them to return to the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.17-Gal.4.20">Gal 4:17-20</reference>. Shows the excellence of the Gospel beyond that of the law, by the allegory of Mount Sinai and Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.21-Gal.4.27">Gal 4:21-27</reference>. Shows also that the believing Gentiles are children of the promise, as Isaac was; and have been elected in the place of the Jews, who have been cast out according to the Scriptures, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.28-Gal.4.31">Gal 4:28-31</reference>. <div eID="gen49731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49732" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen49732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49733" type="x-p"/> The heir, as long as He is a child - Though he be appointed by his father's will heir of all his possessions yet till he arrive at the legal age he is master of nothing, and does not differ from one of the common domestics.
entries.4efbf38f79c712258863a5e15fbacd7f3cb2d45a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen49733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49734" type="x-p"/> But is under tutors - Επιτροπους· Guardians and governors; οικονομους· those who have the charge of the family. These words are nearly similar; but we may consider the first as executor, the last as the person who superintends the concerns of the family and estate till the heir become of age; such as we call trustee. <div eID="gen49734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49735" type="x-p"/> Until the time appointed of the father - The time mentioned in the father's will or testament.
entries.e16761e66205ec77282ccf7d6e8fe3921f9d07a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen49735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49736" type="x-p"/> Even so we - The whole Jewish people were in a state of nonage while under the law. <div eID="gen49736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49737" type="x-p"/> The elements of the world - A mere Jewish phrase, יסודי עולם הזה yesodey olam hazzeh, "the principles of this world;" that is, the rudiments or principles of the Jewish religion. The apostle intimates that the law was not the science of salvation, it was only the elements or alphabet of it; and in the Gospel this alphabet is composed into a most glorious system of Divine knowledge: but as the alphabet is nothing of itself, unless compounded into syllables, words, sentences, and discourses; so the law, taken by itself, gives no salvation; it contains indeed the outlines of the Gospel, but it is the Gospel alone that fills up these outlines.
entries.cb7d5ab718f6d3d702996fc3247f1ee97cb1310f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen49737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49738" type="x-p"/> When the fullness of the time was come - The time which God in his infinite wisdom counted best; in which all his counsels were filled up; and the time which his Spirit, by the prophets, had specified; and the time to which he intended the Mosaic institutions should extend, and beyond which they should be of no avail. <div eID="gen49738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49739" type="x-p"/> God sent forth his Son - Him who came immediately from God himself, made of a woman, according to the promise, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen 3:15</reference>; produced by the power of God in the womb of the Virgin Mary without any intervention of man; hence he was called the Son of God. See Luke, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.35">Luk 1:35</reference>, and the note there. <div eID="gen49739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49740" type="x-p"/> Made under the law - In subjection to it, that in him all its designs might be fulfilled, and by his death the whole might be abolished; the law dying when the Son of God expired upon the cross.
entries.3ccf99641509af4c5e0bb9b46526ca8fec262e0c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen49740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49741" type="x-p"/> To redeem them - Εξαγορασῃ· To pay down a price for them, and thus buy them off from the necessity of observing circumcision, offering brute sacrifices, performing different ablutions, etc., etc. <div eID="gen49741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49742" type="x-p"/> That we might receive the adoption of sons - Which adoption we could not obtain by the law; for it is the Gospel only that puts us among the children, and gives us a place in the heavenly family. On the nature of adoption see the notes on <reference osisRef="Rom.8.15">Rom 8:15</reference>.
entries.a64974372a4d352aa8101de6a516616bde6100c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen49742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49743" type="x-p"/> And because ye are sons - By faith in Christ Jesus, being redeemed both from the bondage and curse of the law; God - the Father, called generally the first person of the glorious Trinity, hath sent forth the Spirit - the Holy Ghost, the second person of that Trinity, of his Son - Jesus Christ, the third person of the Trinity - crying, Abba, Father! from the fullest and most satisfactory evidence that God, the Father, Son, and Spirit, had become their portion. For the explanation of the phrase, and why the Greek and Syriac terms are joined together here, see the notes on <reference osisRef="Mar.14.36">Mar 14:36</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Rom.8.15">Rom 8:15</reference> (note).
entries.a4cccea080400fbec88563eadd11bd79b7e26389: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen49743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49744" type="x-p"/> Thou art no more a servant - Thou who hast believed in Christ art no longer a slave, either under the dominion of sin or under obligation to the Mosaic ritual; but a son of God, adopted into the heavenly family. <div eID="gen49744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49745" type="x-p"/> And if a son, then an heir - Having a right to the inheritance, because one of the family, for none can inherit but the children; but this heirship is the most extraordinary of all: it is not an heirship of any tangible possession, either in heaven or earth; it is not to possess a part or even the whole of either, it is to possess Him who made all things; not God's works, but God himself: heirs of God through Christ.
entries.66a7d829acb86a0bf1a2b8469723f6d5716f4cdd: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen49745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49746" type="x-p"/> When ye knew not God - Though it is evident, from the complexion of the whole of this epistle, that the great body of the Christians in the Churches of Galatia were converts from among the Jews or proselytes to Judaism; yet from this verse it appears that there were some who had been converted from heathenism; unless we suppose that the apostle here particularly addresses those who had been proselytes to Judaism and thence converted to Christianity; which appears to be most likely from the following verses.
