               <ns0:head>CHAP. IV.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">NOw I say, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> the heir so long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be Lord of all <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle had before determined, that the whole body of such as believed in Jesus Christ, were that seed of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> to which the promise was made; and so Heirs of the promises made to him; yet so that as it is among men, though a child be a great Heir, and Lord of a great Estate, yet while he is under age, he is used like a Servant; so the time of the Law be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing as it were the time of Believers non-age, those who lived in that time were used like Servants.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 But is under tutours and governours until the time appointed of the father <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Heir (mentioned in the former verse,) though he be an Heir of a great Estate; yet is not presently possessed of it; but he is by his Father kept under Tutors and Governours, un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />til the time which he hath appointed when he will be pleased to release him from his Pupillage, and settle some part of his in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />heritance upon him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 paragraph">
                        <ns0:desc>〈1 paragraph〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> elements, of this world <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Such children were all Believers, the Seed of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>; from the first designed to a Gospel Liberty, but that was not to be fully enjoyed, until the fulness of time should come when God intended to send his Son into the world: And during the time of their nonage they were kept under the Law, as a Tutor and Governour, leading them unto Christ. He chiefly intend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the Ceremonial Law; which <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 15.10. <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> calleth a <ns0:hi>yoke,</ns0:hi> which neither they, nor their <ns0:hi>Fathers were able to bear.</ns0:hi> He calls these ordinances the <ns0:hi>Elements of the World</ns0:hi>; so also <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.20. he means that Discipline by which God instructed, and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der which God by <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> at first tutoured the World, that is, the Jews, who were that part of the World to whom God pleased to make his Oracles known. He calls those ritual obser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vances, Elements, or <ns0:hi>Rudiments,</ns0:hi> because they were the first Instructions God gave Believers, leading them to Christ; like the first Elements, or Rudimens in Grammer Learning.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 1.10.</ns0:note> when the fulness of the time was come <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>The time,</ns0:hi> which answered the time appointed of the Earthly Father, mentioned <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 2. when that time came in which God had designed to bring his people into the most perfect state of liberty, which in this Life they are capable of:</ns0:note>, God sent forth his Son made of a woman <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>God sent forth his Son,</ns0:hi> who was existent before, (being brought forth before the Mountains or Hills were setled; <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 8.25.) but not <ns0:hi>sent forth</ns0:hi> until this fulness of time came. And then</ns0:note>

                     <ns0:hi>Made under the Law,</ns0:hi> to which as God he was not subject, (being himself the Law<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />maker;) but he subjected himself. Nothing of this is questioned, except the last<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which yet appears also to have been necessary by what followeth in the next verse; for how else could he have redeemed those, who were under the Law, and this agreeth with what we had, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 3.13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 To redeem then that were under the law <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This makes it appear, that Christ's being <ns0:hi>under the law</ns0:hi> must be understood as well of the Moral as of the Ceremonial Law, that is, subject to the precepts of it, as well as to the curse of it: For if the end of this being <ns0:hi>born under the Law,</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deem those that were under it,</ns0:hi> that he had not reached by being merely under the Ceremonial Law, For the Gentiles were not under that Law, but only under the Moral Law;</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 1.12, chap. 3.26.</ns0:note> that we might receive the adoption of sons <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">and they also were to be redeemed, and to receive the great priviledge of <ns0:hi>Adoption,</ns0:hi> or rather, <ns0:hi>the rights</ns0:hi> of adopted children; which (some think) is to be understood here, rather than what is strictly to be understood by the term of Adoption, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> a right to be called, and to be the Sons of God. Others by Adoption understand that full state of liberty which the Apostle had been before speaking, in opposition to that state of childhood and non-age in which believers were until the times of the Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel; for <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 5.1. we shall find that that was a liberty where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />with Christ made us free: And indeed this last sence seemeth best to agree with what the Apostle had before said, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 1, 2, 3. (though the other senses are not to be excluded.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And because you are sons <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Lest the Jews should claim the Adoption as peculiar to them, the Apostle tells them that these Gentiles were also Sons, and in confirmation of that, he saith,</ns0:note>, God hath sent forth <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 8.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, cry<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Abba, Father <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">that God had sent <ns0:hi>the Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit of his Son</ns0:hi> into their hearts: Not that the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> as well as of <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi>; but he calleth him the <ns0:hi>Spirit of Christ,</ns0:hi> because he had made Adoption the end, and fruit of <ns0:hi>Redemption</ns0:hi>; and Redemption is every where made the work of the Son.                      <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the Jews were the first People whom God dignified with the name of his <ns0:hi>Sons,</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>first-born, Exod.</ns0:hi> 4.22. and so many of them as believed also received the Spirit<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 36.27. but the full effusion of the Spirit was re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served to Gospel times, and until the time that Christ Ascend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 7.39. and 16.7<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> After which the Spirit was pour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed out in the days of <ns0:hi>Pentecost, Acts<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:hi> 2. whose effects were evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dent, not only in <ns0:hi>power</ns0:hi> to work miracles, and speak with <ns0:hi>di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers tongues,</ns0:hi> (which were not common to all believers;) but also in a variety of spiritual gifts and habits, amongst which this was one teaching them to cry, <ns0:hi>Abba Father.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>

                     <ns0:hi>Crying</ns0:hi> it is expounded <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.15. <ns0:hi>whereby we cry,</ns0:hi> that is, through whose influence and working in us we cry <ns0:hi>Abba Father,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>Father, Father:</ns0:hi> which not onely signifieth the Spirits influence upon believers words in Prayer, first conceived in the heart, then uttered by the lips, but chiefly those <ns0:hi>

                        </ns0:gap>abits of Grace,</ns0:hi> by which we pray acceptably<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>

                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>es<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and Strangers to God; and a certain evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence of their concern in the Redemption of Christ, and that they also might expect Salvation from him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:480" />7 Wherefore thou <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Thou that art a believing Gentile, as well as the believ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:hi>Israelites.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> art no more a servant <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Art <ns0:hi>no more a Servant,</ns0:hi> not in that state of ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e subjection to the Law:</ns0:note>, but a son <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">but in a more excellent state of liberty; like unto that of Sons that have attained to a full, and ripe age. Christ told his Disciples, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 15.15. that he did not call them Servants, for Servants, knew not what their Lord did; but he had freely communicated to them what he had re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceived from the Father. The Apostle here saith, they were <ns0:hi>sons,</ns0:hi> sons by Adoption; which is the highest notion of freedom and liberty.</ns0:note>, and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">And this entituled them to an inheritance; <ns0:hi>if Sons then Heires.</ns0:hi> Which agreeth with <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.17. and as it is with Sons and Heirs, though the Inheritance cometh not fully to them till the death of the Parent, yet while they live they are in a far better condition then <ns0:hi>Servants</ns0:hi>: so the believing Gentiles be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing made Sons and Heirs of God through Christ, though they were to stay a while for the Inheritance reserved for the Sons of God in the Heavens, yet their state was much better then that of Servants; for though they were obliged to serve the Lord, yet they served him without servile fear, and were no other<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wise Servants then <ns0:hi>Sons</ns0:hi> are also Servants to their Father.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Howbeit then when ye knew not God <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">When ye <ns0:hi>knew not God,</ns0:hi> as he is, or as ye ought to have known him, or as since, you have known him, (for even the Heathen have some knowledge of God, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.21.)</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 12.2. Eph. 2.11, 12.</ns0:note> ye did service unto them which by nature are no gods <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">You paid religious homages unto Idols: which are Gods, not by na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, and essence, but only in the opinion of Idolaters. Which was a more miserable bondage and servitude then the Jews were under, who knew the true God; though in the time, when the Church was like the Heir under age, it was subject to the Law contained in Ordinances, and under the yoke of the Law.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 But now <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 8.3. and 13.12.</ns0:note> after that you have known God <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">After that you are come to a true, and saving knowledge of God in Christ, and know God as he is.</ns0:note>, or rather are known of God <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or rather after you are received of God, approved of him, made through Christ acceptable to him, which is much more then a true comprehen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion of God in your notion and understanding.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col. 2.20.</ns0:note> how turn ye <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>back.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> again to <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 7.18.</ns0:note> the weak and beggarly <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Rudiments.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">How turn you back again to the legal services of the Ceremonial Law, which he calleth <ns0:hi>Elements</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Rudiments,</ns0:hi> because they were Gods first instructions given to his Church for his Worship, to which he intended afterward a more perfect way of Worship. He calls them <ns0:hi>weak</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> because they brought nothing to perfection; and the observance of them was impotent as to the Justification of a Soul, as all the Law is. He calls them <ns0:hi>beggerly</ns0:hi> in comparison of the more rational, spiritual way of worship under the Gospel.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He saith that they <ns0:hi>desired to be in bondage unto these,</ns0:hi> because they would not see and make use of the liberty from them, which Christ had purchased. <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> It may be objected, that the <ns0:hi>Galatians</ns0:hi> were not educated in <ns0:hi>Iudaism</ns0:hi>; how then doth the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle charge them with turning back to them? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> This hath made some think, that, by the <ns0:hi>weak,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>beggerly Elements</ns0:hi> mentioned in this verse, the Apostle meaneth their Gentile superstitions and idolatries; but this is not probable, the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle all along the Epistle charging them with no such Apostacy. Others think, that he in this verse chiefly reflecteth on the believing Jews, who afterwards returned again to the use of the Law. But why may not we rather say, that he calleth their fact a <ns0:hi>turning back,</ns0:hi> not so much with reference to their perso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nal practice, as to the <ns0:hi>State of the Church</ns0:hi>; which was once un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der those Elements, but by the coming of Christ was brought into a more perfect state. So that for them who were called in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the Church in the time of this its more perfect state, for them to return to the bondage of the Law, that was truly <ns0:hi>to turn back</ns0:hi>; if not to any practise of their own, which they had cast off, yet to a state of the Church, which the Church of God had now outgrown.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 14.5. Col. 2.16.</ns0:note> Ye observe dayes <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">If we had any evidence that these <ns0:hi>Galatians</ns0:hi> were relapsed to their Gentile superstitions, these terms might be understood of such days, &c. as they kept in honour to their Idols. But the Apostle throughout the whole Epistle, not reflecting upon them for any such gross Apostacy, (as returning to the vanities of the Heathen in which they formerly lived;) but onely for Judaizing, and using the ceremonies of the Jewish Law, as ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary to be observed, besides their believing in Christ, for their Justification; it is much more probable that he mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth by <ns0:hi>dayes</ns0:hi> the Jewish Festivals: such as their <ns0:hi>New Moons,</ns0:hi> &c. By</ns0:note>, and months <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Moneths,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>first</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>seventh</ns0:hi> moneth, when they religiously fasted.</ns0:note>, and times <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Times,</ns0:hi> their more solemn times such as were their Feasts of <ns0:hi>First-Fruites, Tabernacles,</ns0:hi> &c. And by</ns0:note>, and years <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Years,</ns0:hi> th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>r years of <ns0:hi>Iubilee,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>seventh</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>fiftieth Year.</ns0:hi> His meaning is, that they took themselves to be under a religious obligation to observe these Times as still commanded by God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> knew that with reference to himself, he had not la<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />boured in vain; he might say with <ns0:hi>Isaiah, Though Israel be not gathered, yet</ns0:hi> I <ns0:hi>shall be glorified.</ns0:hi> He had told the <ns0:hi>Corinthians,</ns0:hi> that he knew he should be a <ns0:hi>sweet savour to God,</ns0:hi> as well them that perished as in them that should be saved: but he speaks with reference to them. A faithful Minister accounteth his labour lost when he seeth no Fruits of it upon the Souls of his People. Nor was <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> afraid of this as to the sincerer part of this Church, who truly believed, and were justified, but he speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth this with <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> to the whole Body of this Church. That which he <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, was their falling back from their pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fession of Christianity to <ns0:hi>Iudaism</ns0:hi>; as judging the observation of the Jewish dayes necessary by Divine precept to Christians. Nor doth he speak of the observation of such dayes, as was their duty in obedience to the Moral Law to observe, which com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mandeth the observation of a seventh day for the weekly sab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bath, and gives a liberty for setting apart other dayes, and the commanding the observation of them, to take notice of, and acknowledge God in emergent Providences. But he only speaks of dayes imposed by the Ceremonial Law, and mens religious ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />servation of them as being tyed to it by a Divine precept; by which they made them a part of Worship. We have a liberty to set apart any day for Gods Worship, and Magistrates have a liberty to set apart particular dayes for the acknowledgement of God in emergent Providences, whether of Mercy or Judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment. But none hath a power to make a day holy, so as that it shall be a sin against God for all to labour therein, much less hath any a liberty to keep Jewish Holy-days.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Brethren, I beseech you be as I <ns0:hi>am,</ns0:hi> for I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> as ye <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Be as friendly to me as I am to you, (see the like phrase, 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 22.4.)</ns0:note>, you <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 2.5.</ns0:note> have not injured me at all <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">But how doth the Apostle say they had not <ns0:hi>injured him at all</ns0:hi>? When it is manifest they had defamed him. <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> He had forgiven, or was ready to forgive this to them; he had no desire or design to be reveng'd on them, Or in this particular thing of <ns0:hi>Iudaizing,</ns0:hi> for which he had been <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />flecting upon them, they had done him no personal injury, it was only his care for, and love to their Souls, which had drawn out this discourse from him; not any particular prejudice to them, or any desire he had to take any revenge upon them, for any personal injury done to himself.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Ye know how <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 2.3.</ns0:note> through infirmitie of the flesh I preached the gospel to you at the first <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Scripture having not given us a particular account of <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> circumstances, when he first preached the Gospel to the <ns0:hi>Galatians</ns0:hi>; we are at a loss to determine what those infir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mities were which <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> here speaketh of; more then that he calls them <ns0:hi>infirmities of the flesh.</ns0:hi> By which may be understood, either the baseness, and contemptibleness of his presence, (which the false Teachers at <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> objected to him, 2 <ns0:hi>Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rinthians chapter</ns0:hi> 10. <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 10.) Or some boldly sickness which <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> had at that time, (as some of the antients guesse<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>) or his sufferings for the Gospel, which were those <ns0:hi>infirmitus</ns0:hi> where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in he chose to glory, 2 <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> 11.30.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And my temptation which was in my flesh ye despised not, nor rejected <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The Apostle saith they were so far from <ns0:hi>injuring</ns0:hi> him (as he had said <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 12.) that they had expressed great kindness to him: For though when he first came amongst them to Preach the Gospel, he was a man of no great presence; but, in the judgment of some, vise and base<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> or was full of bodily weakness and diseases; was persecuted by men. Yet they did not <ns0:hi>reject</ns0:hi> nor despise him, for those <ns0:hi>temptations he had in the Flesh:</ns0:hi> by which he means, the same things he before meant by infirmities, for both bodily weaknesses, and sufferings for the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel, are <ns0:hi>Temptations,</ns0:hi> as the word signifieth <ns0:hi>Trials.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, but received me <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mal. 2.7.</ns0:note> as an angel of God, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 10.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> as Christ Jesus <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Nay (saith he) you were so far from rejecting, or despising me up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on that account, that (on the contrary) you received me, as if I had been an Angel; yea, if Jesus Christ himself had came amongst you, you could not have been more kind to him then you were to me.                   </ns0:note> Where is then the blessedness you spake of <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Some understand the <ns0:hi>blessedness</ns0:hi> here spoken of in a passive sense; you were then a blessed and happy people, receiving the Doctrine of the Gospel in the Truth and Purity of it; what is now become of that blessedness?                      </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> you <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">They would exclude you from our good opinion and affection.</ns0:note>, that you might affect them <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">That they might have all your love, and respect; and so by the ruine of our reputation with you, they might build up their own reputation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 But <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> good to be zealously affected al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ways in a good thing <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The Apostle in the former verses had been speaking of a great zeal, or warmth of affection, (for that zeal signifieth,) which these <ns0:hi>Galatians</ns0:hi> had for, and declared towards him, when he first preached the Gospel amongst them; and also of a great warmth and degree of affection which these false Teachers had pretended to this Church. These words are so delivered that they are applicable to either of these; but the latter words seem to make them most properly applicable to the former; so the term [<ns0:hi>alwayes</ns0:hi>] is <ns0:hi>emphatical</ns0:hi>: There was a time, when you were very warm in your love to me; the cause being good, your warmth of affection ought not to have abated, but continued always, and not</ns0:note>, and not only when I am present with you <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">onely while you saw me, and I was <ns0:hi>present with you.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 4.15. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 10. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 1.18.</ns0:note> My little children <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">By calling them <ns0:hi>little Children,</ns0:hi> he both hints to them that he was their Spiritual Father, and had begotten them to Christ; and that they were as yet weak in the Faith, not grown men, but as yet little Children: and also hints to them, the tender affection he had towards them; which was the same as of a mother to her little children: though they did not own and honour him as their spiritual Father, yet he loved them as his <ns0:hi>little Children.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> of whom I travel in birth again <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">For whom I am in as great pain, through my earnest desire for the good of your Souls, as the Woman is that is in travail for the bringing forth of a Child.</ns0:note>, until Christ be formed in you <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Till <ns0:hi>Christ be</ns0:hi> fully and perfectly <ns0:hi>formed in you</ns0:hi>: that is, till you be brought off from your <ns0:hi>Iudaisme,</ns0:hi> and opinion of the necessity of superadding the works of the Law to the Faith of Christ in order to your Justification, and be rooted in the Truth and established in the liberty of the Gospel, with which Christ hath made you free.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 I desire to be present with you now <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">I wish circumstances so concurred that I could be <ns0:hi>present with you.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and to change my voice <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">That I might use my tongue towards you as I saw occasion; either commending, or reproving, or exhorting, as I saw cause.</ns0:note> for, I <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>am perplex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed for you.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> stand in doubt of you <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">For I do not know what to think of you; I am afraid of your falling away from the profession of the Gospel to Judaism.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Tell me ye that desire to be under the law <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">You that cannot be content to receive Jesus Christ alone, for Justification; but have a mind to maintain a necessity of obedience to the Law of circumcision, and other Judaical Rites;</ns0:note>, do ye not hear the law <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Do ye not hear the Law,</ns0:hi> the Law which curseth every one who continueth not in all that is therein written to do it? or rather the story which follows; which is taken out of one of the Books of the Law, which the Apostle makes a mystical Revela<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of the divine Will, that there should come a time when circumcision should be cast out.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 For it is written, that Abraham had two sons, the one <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 16.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> by a bondmaid, the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 11.11.</ns0:note> other by a free-woman <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The substance of this is written, <ns0:hi>Genesis</ns0:hi> 26. where we read of <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> having <ns0:hi>Ishmael</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Hagar</ns0:hi> his bondwoman; and <ns0:hi>Genesis</ns0:hi> 21.2. where we read of the birth of <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> whom he had by <ns0:hi>Sarah</ns0:hi> who was his Wife.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 But he <ns0:hi>who was</ns0:hi> of the bond-woman <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 9.7, 8.</ns0:note> was born after the flesh <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">They were both (in a sence) born <ns0:hi>after the Flesh, viz.</ns0:hi> in a natural way and course of generation: but <ns0:hi>after the flesh</ns0:hi> is plain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly in this verse opposed to <ns0:hi>by promise:</ns0:hi> and the meaning is, that <ns0:hi>Ish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mael,</ns0:hi> the son of <ns0:hi>Hagar,</ns0:hi> was not that son of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> to whom the <ns0:hi>promise</ns0:hi> was made, that <ns0:hi>in him all the Nations of the Earth should be blessed, Genesis</ns0:hi> 15.4. <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 17.19. <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> is said to have been born <ns0:hi>after the promise,</ns0:hi> either because God gave <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> in complement, or fulfilling of the promise made to him, that he should have an Heir out of his own loins; or because the mighty and miraculous power of God was seen in his pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duction, inabling <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> at those years to beget, and <ns0:hi>Sarah</ns0:hi> to bear a child, when both their bodies were as dead.</ns0:note>, but he of the free-woman <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> by promise <ns0:hi>t:</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Which things are an allegory <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">That is called an <ns0:hi>Allegory</ns0:hi> when one thing is learned out of another, or something is mystically signified and to be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood further then is expressed. The Scripture hath a pecu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liar kind of <ns0:hi>Allegories,</ns0:hi> wherein one thing is signified by and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der another thing. The thing here signifying, was <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> Wife and Concubine, <ns0:hi>Sarah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Hagar.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>; For these are the two <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Testaments.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> covenants <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">The Apostle, saith, these signifyed the <ns0:hi>two Covenants</ns0:hi>; for thats the meaning of, <ns0:hi>are.</ns0:hi>) So as here we have one Text more, where the <ns0:hi>verb substantive</ns0:hi> is put for, <ns0:hi>signifieth</ns0:hi>: and it will be hard to assign a reason why it should not be so interpreted in the institution of the Lords Sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />per; (notwithstanding the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Lutherans</ns0:hi> so earnest con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tending to the contrary.) The very word is here used, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, that is used in the institution of the Lords Supper. Here it is <ns0:hi>these are the two Covenants</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Testaments</ns0:hi>; there, <ns0:hi>this is the New Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venant.</ns0:hi> The Apostle calls them <ns0:hi>two</ns0:hi> Covenants, whereas they were but <ns0:hi>one,</ns0:hi> with reference to the time of their exhibition, and manner of their Administration, in which they much differ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed. Nor must we understand the Apostle as signifying to us by these words, that <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> wrote the History of <ns0:hi>Sarah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Hagar,</ns0:hi> with such a design and intention; but only that that History is very applicable to the two Covenants, and we shall find <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 27. the Apostle justifying this application from the authority of the Prophet <ns0:hi>Isaiah.</ns0:hi> And herein he complied with the general sense of the Jews; who judged that there was not onely a litteral<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but a mystical sense also of those Histories of the Patriarchs.</ns0:note>, the one from the mount <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>Sina.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Sinai, which gendreth to bondage <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The one Covenant was that of the Law delivered from mount <ns0:hi>Sinai,</ns0:hi> this was like <ns0:hi>Hagar,</ns0:hi> for as <ns0:hi>Hagar</ns0:hi> was her self a <ns0:hi>Bond wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man,</ns0:hi> and so her child did partake of the condition of the Mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, and <ns0:hi>Hagar</ns0:hi> bare a Bond Man or Servant; so the Law (which he calls a <ns0:hi>Covenant,</ns0:hi> because of the stipulation of obedience from the people to the Will of God revealed, and declared,) lest those that were under it in a state of bondage or servitude.</ns0:note>, which is Agar.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:481" />25 For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Agar</ns0:hi> the bondwoman fitly represented Mount <ns0:hi>Sinai,</ns0:hi> the Mountain in <ns0:hi>Arabia,</ns0:hi> from which the Law was given:</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>is in the same rank with.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> answereth to Jerusalem which now is <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And <ns0:hi>Ierusalem which now is</ns0:hi> answereth to Mount <ns0:hi>Sinai</ns0:hi>; for as in Mount <ns0:hi>Sinai</ns0:hi> the Law was given in a terrible manner, so now <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> is the seat of the <ns0:hi>Scribes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> who are the Doctors of <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> Law, and rigidly press the observation of it.</ns0:note>, and is in bondage with her children <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">By which the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> are kept <ns0:hi>in bondage:</ns0:hi> The Apostle speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth not here of the civil servitude that the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> were in un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> to whom they were now Tributaries, but of that Religious servitude in which the <ns0:hi>Scribes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> kept them to their legal services.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 2.2. Heb. 12.22. Rev. 3.12. & 21.2, 10.</ns0:note> But Jerusalem which is above, is free <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The new Covenant, or the dispensation of the Gospel, or the Christian Church, which is <ns0:hi>above,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>from above,</ns0:hi> which an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swereth to <ns0:hi>Sarah,</ns0:hi> and is said <ns0:hi>to be above,</ns0:hi> because revealed from Heaven by Christ, sent out of the bosom of the Father, not as the Law was revealed upon Earth, upon Mount <ns0:hi>Sinai.</ns0:hi> Hence Apostates from the Doctrine of the Gospel, are said to turn from him who <ns0:hi>speaketh from Heaven, Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.25. Or else it is said to be <ns0:hi>above,</ns0:hi> because it is the <ns0:hi>assembly of the first born written in Heaven,</ns0:hi> ver. 23. hence the Gospel Church is called the <ns0:hi>Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venly Hierusalem,</ns0:hi> ver. 22. Of this Gospel Church the Apostle saith, that it is <ns0:hi>free, i. e.</ns0:hi> free from the yoke and bondage of the Ceremonial Law, or from the <ns0:hi>Covenant</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>curse of the Law.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, which is the mother of us all <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Which Church he saith is the <ns0:hi>Mother of all Believers,</ns0:hi> they imbracing the same Faith, and walking in the same steps, from whence was easie for the <ns0:hi>Galatians</ns0:hi> to conclude, their freedom and liberty also from the Law.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 For it is written, Rejoyce thou barren that bearest not, break forth and cry, thou that tra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vailest not, for the desolate hath many mo chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren, then she which hath an husband <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">It is written <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 54.1. Some think that the Apostle doth but allude to that of the Prophet, and that the sense of the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet was only to comfort the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> whose City, though it should be for a present time barren, thin of Inhabitants, du<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring the time of the <ns0:hi>Babylonish</ns0:hi> Captivity; yet it should be a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gain replenished with people, and be more populous then other Cities. But the Prophet seemeth rather to interpret that Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phesie, then meerly to allude to it; so that verse is one of those Prophetical passages about the calling of the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> (of which are many in that Prophet.) In this sense, the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> are to be understood under the notion of the woman that was <ns0:hi>barren and desolate.</ns0:hi> The Church of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> is represented under the notion of a Woman that had an Husband and Children. The Prophet, by the Spirit of <ns0:hi>Prophesie,</ns0:hi> calleth upon the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> that brought forth no children to God, and to whom God was not an Husband, to <ns0:hi>Rejoyce,</ns0:hi> and to <ns0:hi>cry out for joy,</ns0:hi> for there should be more Believers, more children brought forth to God, amongst them, then were amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews:</ns0:hi> So as the Church of the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> are compared to <ns0:hi>Sarah,</ns0:hi> who was a long time barren, but then brought forth the child of the Promise, the Seed in which all the Nations of the Earth were to be blessed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 Now we, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of promise <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> was the promised Seed, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 21.12. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.8. the Apostle tells the <ns0:hi>Galatians</ns0:hi> that the believing <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> were (as <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi>) the <ns0:hi>children of the promise. Isaac</ns0:hi> being born, not by vertue of any procreative vertue in his <ns0:hi>Parents,</ns0:hi> which was now dead in them, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.19. but by vertue of the promise, and by a power above nature, was a Type of the believing <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> who are a Spiritual Seed, and that <ns0:hi>Seed</ns0:hi> to whom the promise was made, being the Members of Christ by Faith: So as the <ns0:hi>Jews</ns0:hi> had no reason so much to glory as they did, that <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> was their Father, for those amongst them that believed not, were but his carnal Seed, believers only were the Spiritual Seed, the <ns0:hi>children of the Promise:</ns0:hi> To which the believing <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> had the same claim with the believing <ns0:hi>Jews,</ns0:hi> and a much better then those of them that believed not in Christ.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 But as then he that was born after the flesh <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">As it was in <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> time, <ns0:hi>Ishmael,</ns0:hi> who was born in a meer carnal and ordinary way of Generation:</ns0:note>, persecuted him <ns0:hi>that was born</ns0:hi> after the spirit <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Persecuted <ns0:hi>Isaac,</ns0:hi> by mocking at him, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 21.9. who was born by vertue of the promise, and the mighty power of God, inabling <ns0:hi>Sarah</ns0:hi> at those years to conceive, and <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> to beget a Child.</ns0:note>, even so <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> now <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Even so it is now, the carnal Seed of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Jews</ns0:hi> per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />secute the Christians which are his Spiritual Seed. From whence we may observe, that the Holy Ghost accounteth mockings of good people for Religion, Persecution. So <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.36. others had <ns0:hi>tryals of cruel mockings,</ns0:hi> and we know these were one kind of the sufferings of Christ. By this also the Apostle doth both confirm, what he had before said, in making <ns0:hi>Hagar</ns0:hi> a Type of the <ns0:hi>Jews,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sarah</ns0:hi> a Type of the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Jews</ns0:hi> persecu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting the seed of Christ, as <ns0:hi>Hagars</ns0:hi> seed persecuted <ns0:hi>Isaac.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 Nevertheless, what saith the scripture? Cast out the bond-woman and her son, for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 8.35.</ns0:note> the son of the bond-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free-woman <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">We read <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 21.10. that when <ns0:hi>Sarah</ns0:hi> saw <ns0:hi>Ishmael</ns0:hi> mock<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing at her Son <ns0:hi>Isaac,</ns0:hi> she was not able to bear it, but speaketh to her Husband <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> saying, <ns0:hi>Cast out this bond-woman, and her Son, for the Son of this bond-woman shall not be heir with my Son, even</ns0:hi> Isaac. The principal design of the Apostle seems to be, by that Type of the ejection of <ns0:hi>Ishmael</ns0:hi> out of <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> Family, to let them know the mind and will of God. 1. Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning the exclusion of the Law from a partnership with Christ, and the Gospel, in the justification of sinners before God. 2. Concerning the rejection of the <ns0:hi>Jews,</ns0:hi> upon the calling of the <ns0:hi>Gentiles.</ns0:hi> 3. Concerning the total destruction of the Jewish Church and Nation, for their persecution of Christ, and the Christian Church.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 So then brethren, we are not children of the bond-woman, but of the free <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Church of the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> was not Typified in <ns0:hi>Hagar,</ns0:hi> but in <ns0:hi>Sarah</ns0:hi>; from whence the scope of the Apostle is to con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clude, that we are not <ns0:hi>under the Law,</ns0:hi> obliged to <ns0:hi>Judaical ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />servances,</ns0:hi> but are freed from them, and are justified by Faith in Christ alone, not by the works of the Law. By this conclusi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, the Apostle maketh way for the exhortation in the fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing chapter, pressing them to stand fast in their liberty.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
